title: Should Scotland’s Lord Advocate keep both jobs?
label: 18 November 2026 · The Lord Advocate’s dual role
summary: Former Lord Advocate Lord Mulholland argued that Scotland benefits from having one person serve as the Government’s chief legal adviser and head of prosecutions. He said the arrangement helps Ministers avoid harming investigations and lets prosecution experience shape laws. Committee members pressed him on perceived conflicts, private contact with Ministers, appointments and public safeguards. He said he had experienced no political interference, opposed splitting the roles, but supported writing down the rules on when Law Officers step aside from cases.

speakers.label: Chair
speakers.name: Patricia Ferguson
speakers.role: Chair of the Scottish Affairs Committee

speakers.label: Lord Mulholland
speakers.name: Lord Mulholland
speakers.role: Former Lord Advocate and former Solicitor General for Scotland

glossary.definition: Scotland’s chief prosecutor and the Scottish Government’s principal legal adviser.
The Scottish Law Officer who assists the Lord Advocate and can act in their place.
A senior government legal office-holder, such as Scotland’s Lord Advocate or Solicitor General.
Senior Scottish prosecutors who make decisions about serious criminal cases.
The 1998 law that established Scotland’s devolved Parliament and Government and sets out some of their powers.
The general rule against trying someone again for a crime after they have been acquitted, subject to legal exceptions.
The person who chairs meetings of the Scottish Parliament and oversees its proceedings.
A member of the Scottish Parliament.

chapters.title: Why combine the roles?
chapters.takeaway: Lord Mulholland said direct access to Ministers helps protect investigations and turn prosecutors’ experience into better laws.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What’s the advantage of having the Lord Advocate both advise the Scottish Government on law and lead prosecutions?

evidence.quote: what do you think are the main advantages of the devolved Law Officers having that dual role as both the Government’s legal advisers and the senior prosecutor?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Ministers need to speak to the public after major events, but they mustn’t say anything that could damage an investigation. After the Glasgow airport bombing and the Clutha helicopter crash, we could quickly tell them what they could and couldn’t say.

evidence.quote: If you remember the Glasgow airport bombing, the First Minister rang the relevant Cabinet Secretaries, who were all quickly advised what they could and could not say.

Another example was the Clutha helicopter crash. All these examples were in my time as a Law Officer. Again, you needed to speak to them quickly so they knew what they could and could not say. Of course, as politicians it is incumbent on them to give reassurance and information to the public

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Leading prosecutions also lets you spot gaps in the law. A terrorism investigation exposed problems coordinating cases across Scotland and England because their prosecution deadlines differed. I raised that with the UK Government, which later changed the law for cross-border terrorism cases. I also alerted the First Minister when Scotland lacked legislation covering the sharing of intimate images.

evidence.quote: the prosecution authorities down south applied different timescales than in Scotland. It is 110 days to 140 days to 12 months in Scotland; it is a lot longer—I do not know what it is now, but it certainly was at that time—down south. So the two investigations were clashing and eventually no proceedings were taken.
I talked to the UK Government and in 2008—I think it was—they made a provision in the relevant Counter-Terrorism Act for universal jurisdiction in Scotland.
There was no legislation covering that in Scotland at the time. I spoke publicly about it and spoke to the First Minister to alert him to the issue. Of course, there is now legislation in Scotland.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: When I travelled to Libya to pursue the Lockerbie investigation, the First Minister needed to know where I was in case something happened. That didn’t mean discussing the evidence with him. It’s another example of why the head of prosecutions sometimes needs a direct, confidential conversation with the First Minister.

evidence.quote: I went to Tripoli with Robert Mueller to Tripoli two or three months after the fall of Gaddafi; Libya was just coming out of a war.

the First Minister has to know what you are doing because if something happened, it would be worldwide news. You have to be able to have a conversation with the First Minister on Privy Council terms so that he knows what you are doing. I am not discussing the evidence with him, but he needs to know.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: So, on balance, should those two roles be split?

evidence.quote: On balance, and based on your experience in the role, should the dual role be split?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: No. You’d lose prosecutors’ direct input into new laws and Government decisions, including the ability to warn Ministers quickly not to prejudice a live investigation.

evidence.quote: No.

you would not have what I have just described—that input into Government policy and new legislation, or input into Ministers to make sure that they do not say things that are going to prejudice an inquiry.

chapters.title: Independence and its appearance
chapters.takeaway: Members questioned whether combining the jobs creates conflicts even without interference; Lord Mulholland distinguished that concern from what he experienced.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: What are the risks of giving the same Law Officers both jobs?

evidence.quote: what are the main risks or disadvantages that come with the Law Officers having a dual role?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: People may suspect political motives. History gives them reason to ask questions: there were political prosecutions centuries ago. But the Scotland Act protects the independence of prosecution and death investigations. In my nine years as a Law Officer, no politician ever asked me to discuss evidence in a live case.

evidence.quote: I suppose the risk is that people think you have malign intentions or political intentions.
During the French revolution, there were a lot of political prosecutions for sedition.
the exercise of the retained functions of the Lord Advocate, such as investigations of deaths and prosecutions, are guaranteed to be independent.
I never had one approach by an MSP, MP, Government Minister or First Minister wanting to discuss the evidence in live cases—not once.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: Even if people are entitled to worry about information crossing from prosecutions into politics, is it frustrating when they assume that happens?

evidence.quote: People are entitled to their perceptions, but is there a frustration at the perception people have that there is leakage across the information barrier, because that would never happen?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Yes. No information about criminal cases leaked that way during my time. I told Ministers only what I judged they needed to know. I went to roughly one in four Government Cabinet meetings, generally when legal advice or another legal matter was on the agenda. Neither I nor the Solicitor General attended the separate political Cabinet meetings.

evidence.quote: There is a frustration, I suppose, that some people do not understand that and some people do not accept it. The reality is that there was no leakage of information in relation to criminal cases during my time as Lord Advocate and Solicitor General. You would tell the First Minister or the Cabinet what they needed to know.
from memory I attended about one in four. That was the Government Cabinet. There were two Cabinets—a Government Cabinet and a political Cabinet.
I never attended any, and the Solicitor General did not attend any, because they were political
If there was something I had given legal advice on, I would be there to answer any questions about that legal advice. If there was something legal on the Cabinet agenda, I would attend

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If an MSP were suspected of a crime and neither Law Officer made the prosecution decision, could a Law Officer still answer questions about it in Parliament?

evidence.quote: there might be occasions when the Lord Advocate, having not been involved in a case because it was not considered appropriate for them to be involved, would still answer questions in the Scottish Parliament about that case?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Yes. The Law Officer answering would need a briefing, even if they hadn’t decided the case. It might simply explain why answering a particular question could harm the proceedings. An independent senior member of Crown Counsel would decide whether to prosecute.

evidence.quote: whichever Law Officer is answering questions will need to be briefed. The brief might be why you cannot answer that question, because it may prejudice proceedings or be contrary to the interests of justice.
It would be independent Crown Counsel. A senior member of Crown Counsel would be given the papers to take a decision on the case. They are not a politician or a Law Officer

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Isn’t that a weakness of the dual role? Even if no one interferes politically, you sometimes step away from decisions because a reasonable person might see a conflict.

evidence.quote: Is that not the problem with the dual role? You have given all these examples of where there is a perception of conflict. These other obstacles and barriers are then put in place, which are the various recusals.
It is not that there is actual political interference; it is that the reasonable person test must be considered.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I understand the concern, but the established practice of stepping aside when an MP or MSP is involved doesn’t prove political interference. In one case involving an MSP, independent Crown Counsel made the decision; I didn’t even know at the time who had made it. I’ve never had a politician interfere in a prosecution decision.

evidence.quote: The only recusal that I am aware of was an MSP or MP—there may be others that I have overlooked.
I have never had any political interference in any decision that I have had and have never discussed live cases with any politician.

When it was decision-making time, that was sent to independent Crown Counsel. When that decision was then announced, because live proceedings were taken, I was asked questions about bias. At the time, I did not even know who had taken the decision.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But might the public still find it strange that you could answer questions about a case you’d deliberately stayed out of?

evidence.quote: You may, however, be asked to answer a question about it in Parliament. Does that not give rise to a public perception that something in the nature of this is a wee bit strange and that perhaps these roles need to be split for that reason?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: To an extent. But Law Officers already make it clear in their parliamentary answers when independent Crown Counsel, rather than a Law Officer, took the decision.

evidence.quote: You may have a point to a certain extent

it is kind of standard practice for the Law Officer, in answering a question, to make that clear: “Can I just advise you? A decision was not taken by a Law Officer because the convention applies; it was taken by independent Crown Counsel.”

chapters.title: Contact with Ministers and clearer rules
chapters.takeaway: Lord Mulholland defended some direct conversations with Ministers, while accepting that written guidance on stepping aside from cases could help the public.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: What actually stops political interference? Would splitting the jobs add oversight when things go wrong?

evidence.quote: Are formalised safeguards in place to ensure that there can never be political interference in a case?
Would it not be better if the dual role was split, so that there was some additional oversight when things aren’t quite going as they should?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: The law protects independent decisions, and experienced Crown Office staff advise Law Officers about what they can say and do. I don’t think splitting the roles would improve perceptions: those legal protections and working practices are already there. I experienced no attempted political interference.

evidence.quote: There are statutory provisions that guard against political interference. Of course, the structure of the Crown Office and the private office is set up to apply the legislation.
You will have quite a large team, in Crown Office terms, briefing Lords Advocate as to what they can and cannot say.
Would it improve people’s perceptions? I don’t think so, because the structures and procedures are in place to ensure independence.
Did someone attempt it? No. No, I didn’t experience that.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Were your conversations with the First Minister always formally recorded, or did you also talk by phone?

evidence.quote: Is everything on a formal footing? You mentioned that you had to call the First Minister before you made a trip to Libya. Was everything formalised, or would there be a phone call chatting about things that were going on?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: It was a mixture. I sometimes spoke in person or by phone; before Libya, I didn’t want a written note to leak and endanger the trip. We didn’t chat about live cases. When the First Minister sought formal legal advice, the request and my answer would normally be in writing.

evidence.quote: that was a phone call or a face-to-face conversation, because I did not want anything in writing before I went, in case it leaked out or got FOI-ed.
It is a mixture. If it is formal, it will be in a minute across to the First Minister’s office. You do chat from time to time about things, not about live cases.
if it is a legal matter, you would expect it in writing, and your answer would be in writing.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Would requiring those conversations to be formally recorded reduce the appearance of a conflict?

evidence.quote: Would an improved safeguard be the strengthening of the formal arrangement between the Lord Advocate and the First Minister? We spoke about how sometimes there would be calls and chats that were not minuted

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I think that would go too far. After the First Minister publicly criticised judges over a criminal appeal, I went straight to his office and told him not to do it again. I was acting as head of prosecutions, not as his legal adviser. I don’t think I’d have had that quick access if the roles were split.

evidence.quote: In my personal opinion, it would be over the top.

I went to the First Minister’s office first thing the next morning and spoke to him. I am paraphrasing, but I read him the riot act and said that he is not going to say that again—he is not going to criticise judges.
When I told him not to say those things, I was going over as the prosecutor because it related to a criminal case. I would not have had that access to the First Minister if the roles were split.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: In the Andrew Coulson perjury case, how did you prevent political interference or comments that might prejudice the trial?

evidence.quote: What actions or precautions did you take as Lord Advocate to ensure that that criminal case was progressed free from political interference or prejudicial comment?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Crown Counsel made the prosecution decision; I wasn’t involved in it. I did write to senior political and parliamentary figures because I feared public comments could prejudice the case. Those messages contained nothing about the case itself, and there was no public comment.

evidence.quote: It was Crown Counsel that took the decision, and I think it was Crown Counsel, as the decision maker, that prosecuted the case.
I just knew that the prosecution was ongoing; I was not involved in the decision making.

Because there was a fear that they would. Of course, it was not the Crown Counsel that would write to the Prime Minister, the First Minister or the Presiding Officer. It had to be a Law Officer—the Lord Advocate.
There was no public comment and justice took its course.
There is nothing about the case in them.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: Would it help people understand these decisions if the rules for when a Law Officer steps aside from a case were written down?

evidence.quote: I am trying to think whether there should be a process that is written down that everyone can see, just for the sake of transparency, so that everyone can tell why that person has recused themselves or why that person has decided they can take part in it.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: Yes, that could help. The practice for cases involving MPs and MSPs is unwritten; it might be put into law. Written guidance could also address whether it extends to former politicians or party officials. That’s my personal view, though, and the current Lord Advocate would need to consider it.

evidence.quote: The convention—it is unwritten—that Law Officers do not take decisions in criminal cases involving Members of Parliament or Members of the Scottish Parliament could be put in legislation
It would be helpful for the public if this recusal convention, and when you would recuse yourself, was set down on paper.

Does it apply to former MPs or former MSPs? I think a bit of work should be given to it, but that is just a personal opinion; you would need to ask the current Lord Advocate what they thought about that

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Did you ever give Ministers details of a criminal case before those details became public?

evidence.quote: Would you have disclosed to Scottish Ministers any of the specifics of a criminal case that was going through? That might be the timeline or the amount of money involved in an embezzlement case, for example.
if the information was not public at that point, would that still be something that you would have passed on?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I recall one example: after a change in the law on double jeopardy, I formally told the Government that prosecutors were about to ask a court to reopen an acquittal in the World’s End case. I didn’t disclose the evidence or why we’d decided to apply. The application wasn’t public yet, but it was about to be lodged in court.

evidence.quote: when we decided that the evidence met the test, I formally advised that an application would be made to the court to set aside the acquittal. I did not go into the evidence, explain why that decision was taken or explain what the new evidence was
It was not made public at the time that I sent the minute, but it would shortly become public, because the application was about to be lodged with the court.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: For the MSP prosecution I mentioned, I don’t remember sending Ministers a note that a prosecution was coming, and I can’t imagine doing so. I can’t swear no such note was sent.

evidence.quote: I do not think I would, to be honest, because it is a prosecution. I cannot swear to it, but I have no memory of a minute on the MSP case that I mentioned being sent across to Bute House to advise that there was to be a live prosecution. I cannot swear to that, but I cannot imagine me doing that.

chapters.title: Who should hold the office?
chapters.takeaway: Lord Mulholland favoured politically independent legal advisers and extensive experience, while accepting questions about how appointments are made.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: Would the Government be better served by legal advisers who openly belonged to a political party?

evidence.quote: would the Scottish Government benefit from having party political senior legal advisers as is the norm in the UK and Welsh Governments?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: I don’t think so. I’ve never disclosed my political views, and neither First Minister I served asked about them. A political adviser might feel pressure to give the answer the Government wanted. Confidential legal advice should instead say frankly what’s lawful, what isn’t and how a proposal might be made lawful.

evidence.quote: The only person who knows my political views is the ballot box. I have never made them known
Alex Salmond when I was appointed Solicitor General, he did not ask what my political views were or how I voted or anything; Nicola Sturgeon did not ask either.
if you had political legal advisers, then the legal advice that you give could be skewed. You could be trying to please
You give unvarnished legal advice to the Government of the day as to whether something is legal, and, if it is not, what the considerations are and how it could be made legal.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Should appointments be more open and competitive so the public can see how a Lord Advocate is chosen?

evidence.quote: If the public are to have confidence in the dual role of the office, should it not be clear and transparent how the role holder is appointed?
do you not think the public would have more confidence if it was a system of competition, like any other job vacancy, rather than phone calls and meetings in hotels?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: You may have a point. I was unexpectedly approached about becoming Solicitor General, met Alex Salmond and was offered the job that day. Later, after four years doing that job, I was phoned and asked to become Lord Advocate. Other appointments have involved several candidates and interviews, but I don’t think there were other candidates when I was appointed.

evidence.quote: I got a completely unexpected phone call one day from, I think, the Cabinet Secretary for Justice, who asked if I was interested in becoming Solicitor General.
I then went to the Caledonian hotel in Edinburgh, where I met Alex Salmond. We had a chat of about half an hour.
I got a phone call later that day saying, “We are happy to appoint you Solicitor General.”
I got a phone call a few days into the new Government to ask whether I would be Lord Advocate.
with successive Lords Advocate, there has been a process involving interviews and there have been a number of candidates, but that did not apply to me.
You may have a point—I do not know.
I do not think there were any other candidates.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Must the Lord Advocate have spent their career prosecuting cases?

evidence.quote: Do you think the appointment should be made among career prosecutors such as yourself?

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: No, though experience helps. My own prosecution work showed me the need for a unit to reopen unsolved cases, which I set up as Lord Advocate. But the job doesn’t require a career prosecutor: it requires hard work, sound judgment, principles and a determination to improve things.

evidence.quote: Experience helps in doing that job. It is a hell of a job.
I set up the cold case unit in 2011 when I became Lord Advocate, because from my time as a frontline prosecutor, I knew the importance of that.
does the person need to be a prosecutor?—no, they do not. It requires hard work, intellect, principles and a determination to make things better.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How important is it that the Lord Advocate has a Solicitor General who can act for them?

evidence.quote: would the system have been more difficult if the person who is Lord Advocate did not have a formal deputy with full legal powers to act on their behalf
if you didn’t have a Solicitor General, your role would be that much harder.

turns.speaker: Lord Mulholland
turns.text: You need one. The Solicitor General can act for the Lord Advocate when they’re away and can also gain experience for the top job. I think there should be at least one other Law Officer.

evidence.quote: When I was out of the country, the Solicitor General would effectively act as the Lord Advocate.
You need a Solicitor General. The other thing about a Solicitor General is that if they want to step up to become a Lord Advocate, it is a good way to train the next Lord Advocate.
I certainly think that you need another Law Officer at least.
